Sanskrit and scripts

Classical languages of India: all 11 and when they were named

India has 11 classical languages. Tamil was the first, declared in 2004, followed by Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013) and Odia (2014). In October 2024 the Government of India added Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali. The status recognises a long, independently attested literary tradition.

Talaash Heritage runs a lecture on India's linguistic heritage and introductory Prakrit and Pali courses, two of the newest classical languages, for groups online or in person.

What is a classical language in India?

Classical language is a category created by the Government of India in 2004 to recognise languages with a very old, rich and well-attested literary heritage. The decision is taken by the Union government on the advice of an expert committee, and the Ministry of Culture administers it. It is separate from the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, which lists 22 scheduled languages for other purposes.

The status brings support from the Ministry of Education and other bodies: international awards for scholars, centres of excellence for study, and the possibility of professional chairs in universities. It does not change how a language is used in government or schools.

List of the 11 classical languages of India

The table lists all eleven in the order they were recognised. Pali and Prakrit are the only two that are not today the main language of a state, and both are Middle Indo-Aryan languages of ancient India; see Prakrit and Pali.

Tamil2004DravidianTamil-Brahmi inscriptions; Sangam poetry; Tolkappiyam
Sanskrit2005Indo-AryanVedic texts; epics; classical kavya
Telugu2008Dravidianinscriptions from the mid first millennium CE; Nannaya's Mahabharata
Kannada2008DravidianHalmidi inscription; Kavirajamarga
Malayalam2013Dravidianearly inscriptions; Ramacharitam
Odia2014Indo-Aryanearly inscriptions; medieval literature from Sarala Das onward
Marathi2024Indo-Aryanearly inscriptions; Dnyaneshwari
Pali2024Indo-Aryan (Middle)Theravada Buddhist canon
Prakrit2024Indo-Aryan (Middle)Ashokan edicts; Jain Agamas; Prakrit poetry
Assamese2024Indo-AryanCharyapada links; medieval literature; Sankardev's works
Bengali2024Indo-AryanCharyapada links; Middle Bengali literature

Which was the first classical language of India?

Tamil was the first, declared in 2004. Its claim rests on a literature that is both very old and independent of Sanskrit: the Sangam anthologies of poetry, usually dated to roughly the early centuries BCE and CE, the grammar Tolkāppiyam, and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in caves and on pottery. Debates about the exact dates of the Sangam texts continue, but their antiquity is not in doubt.

Sanskrit followed in 2005. Its case rests on the Vedic texts, the epics and an unbroken learned tradition of more than three thousand years; the what is Sanskrit guide covers its history. Together Tamil and Sanskrit represent the two great classical traditions of the subcontinent, Dravidian and Indo-Aryan.

Criteria for classical language status

When the category was created, the criteria included high antiquity of early texts or recorded history, a body of ancient literature regarded as valuable heritage, and an original literary tradition not borrowed from another speech community. The required antiquity was raised from about 1,000 years to about 1,500 to 2,000 years in 2005. The criteria were reviewed again in 2024, when the five new languages were added. The current wording, as published by the Ministry of Culture, should be checked on official sources, since such criteria are revised from time to time.

Several of these languages are first attested in inscriptions, which is why epigraphy carries so much weight in the evidence. The what is epigraphy guide explains how inscriptions are read and dated.

The October 2024 additions

On 3 October 2024 the Union Cabinet approved classical status for Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali, the largest single addition so far. Marathi's case drew on early inscriptions and medieval literature including the Dnyaneshwari. The inclusion of Pali and Prakrit was significant because they are not regional mother tongues today but were the languages of Ashoka's edicts, early Buddhist and Jain scripture, and much ancient poetry.

These additions underline how much of India's early written record is not in Sanskrit at all. Ashoka's inscriptions, in Prakrit and Brahmi script, are among the oldest datable documents of Indian history.

Studying India's classical languages

For most learners the best entry point is the history that connects these languages: how Indo-Aryan and Dravidian traditions developed side by side, borrowed from each other and shared scripts descended from Brahmi. The linguistic heritage lecture covers exactly that. For hands-on study, Talaash Heritage offers short introductory courses in Prakrit and Pali, two of the newest classical languages, alongside a Brahmi workshop and a Sharada script course.

Questions people ask

How many classical languages are there in India?

Eleven: Tamil, Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali. The last five were added in October 2024.

Which was the first language to be declared classical in India?

Tamil, in 2004. Sanskrit was declared the next year, in 2005, followed by Telugu and Kannada in 2008, Malayalam in 2013 and Odia in 2014.

Which languages got classical status in 2024?

Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali, approved by the Union Cabinet on 3 October 2024. This raised the total number of classical languages of India from six to eleven.

Is Hindi a classical language?

No. Hindi is an official language of the Union and one of the 22 scheduled languages, but it is a relatively modern language in the classical-language sense and does not have classical status. Its older relatives, Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit, do.

What benefits does classical status give a language?

Mainly support for scholarship: national and international awards for eminent scholars, centres of excellence for study, and the possibility of professional chairs in universities, administered with the Ministry of Education. It does not alter the language's use in administration or schooling.
